abstract_text: An amphibian survey was initiated at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas to assess anecdotal observations of anuran population declines. In February 1998, 350 meters of PVC pipe were installed at selected sites to evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in regard to hylid frog populations. These and other sites are currently being monitored in order to gain insight to amphibian population dynamics at Brazos Bend State Park.

title: Amphibian species distribution patterns in an agriculturally-fragmented landscape

authors.affiliation: Dept. Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907-1159, USA
Dept. Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907-1159, USA

abstract_text: Apparent declines of amphibian populations in many parts of the world have caused great concern in recent years. This study was conducted to determine what effects agriculturally induced fragmentation of forests has had on amphibian assemblages and their distribution in a midwestern landscape. Potential breeding pools and upland areas in 30 forest patches of various sizes and degrees of isolation were intensively sampled for amphibians from April through August 1996 and March through August 1997. Species presence was documented by using pitfall trapping, anuran vocalization surveys, cover board sampling, minnow traps, and dipnetting for larva. Amphibian, anuran and salamander assemblages were all nonrandomly distributed across the landscape. Bufo americanus and Hyla versicolor were ubiquitous whereas the distribution of several species including Ambystoma tigrinum, A. texanum, Plethodon cinereus, Rana clamitans, and R. pipiens showed significant nesting. Overall, species richness was significantly associated with a weighted measure of wetland permanency (WETWGT, p=0.0001, WETWGTC2, p=0.0029), with forest patches which have seasonal and semi-permanent wetlands containing more species. Abundance of amphibians was significantly associated with forest proximity (LOGPR, p=0.0001, LOGPRC2, p=0.0037), with more isolated patches having greater amphibian abundance. The observed distribution and degree of nestedness exhibited by several amphibians suggests that these species respond to landscape-level factors.

title: Response of the herpetofaunal community to three sandhill restoration treatments on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida

authors.affiliation: Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, University of Florida, Box 110430, Gainesville, FL 32611-0430

abstract_text: The longleaf pine ecosystem, once widespread in the southeastern United States, has been reduced by as much as 98%. Restoration of this endangered ecosystem can be a mechanism for conservation, in an attempt to reverse existing damage and create more resilient communities. Restoration methods implemented in sandhills must be based in a deep knowledge of the ecosystem to effectively recreate and manage all aspects. Consequently, restoration success can only be evaluated by examining community response. Since reptiles and amphibians occupy the ecosystem at a fairly small scale, these communities may be important indicators of microhabitat restoration success. Previous work on herpetofaunal response to disturbance regimes has demonstrated the complexity of the effects and the importance of habitat structure. Habitat requirements for sandhill herpetofauna are very diverse, demonstrating the need to closely examine these communities when making management decisions. My study, which focuses on reptiles and amphibians, is one portion of a multi-agency investigation of three sandhill restoration techniques on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida: fire, oak-specific herbicide, and mechanical oak felling. Pitfall traps and drift fences were used to capture reptiles and amphibians in restoration treatment areas, control plots and 'typical' longleaf pine sandhill areas during the summer of 1997. Animals were identified to species, marked, sexed, weighed, measured, and visually examined. Vegetative cover data were also collected. The objective of this project is to examine herpetofaunal species richness and abundance, as well as population age class structure and sex ratios, with regards to the restoration treatment and vegetative structure.

title: Anuran assemblages in anthropogenically and pyrogenically disturbed landscapes of the boreal forest

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Victoria, PO Box 3020 STN CSC, Victoria BC V8W 3N5, Canada

abstract_text: Alberta-Pacific Forest Industries Inc. (AL-PAC) operates a large pulp mill in the mixed-wood boreal forest of northeastern Alberta. The company harvests within its 6,000,000 ha Forest Management Area (FMA) using an 'ecosystem management' perspective. In other words, AL-PAC attempts to mimic fire, the dominant natural disturbance of the boreal forest. Five amphibian species, including two that appear to have undergone population declines, occur in the FMA. In 1997, I sampled anuran communities at 12 lakes to investigate whether each species showed the same relative abundance in logged, naturally burned, and undisturbed areas. I employed call surveys, transect sampling, egg and larval searches, and metamorph searches. Additionally, I conducted vegetation surveys on each transect to quantitatively examine differences in habitat. Preliminary results suggest that lakes with adjacent cutblocks support the highest number of amphibians; however, this may be a function of lake size, distance from active roads, or forest type. An analysis to separate these effects is underway.

title: The effects of forest-pasture edges on the herpetofauna of Fila Cruces, Costa Rica

authors.affiliation: Department of Natural Resources, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-3001, USA

abstract_text: Human activities tend to create highly fragmented landscapes, thereby exposing remaining habitat to the effects of edges. I am interested in the impacts of forest-pasture edges on the dynamics of frog and lizard populations. Using a paired-plot design, I described the abundance and distribution of lizards (Norops spp.) and leaf-litter frogs (Eleutherodactylus spp.) in 10 forest fragments near Las Cruces, Costa Rica. The study took place from February to June, 1997, and covered both dry and wet seasons. No species was definitively absent from the edge plots. Nocturnal leaf-litter frogs were generally equally abundant near forest edges and in forest interiors. The single diurnal eleutherodactylid species, however, was consistently more abundant in the forest interiors, suggesting that abiotic edge effects may be stronger during the day than at night. Anoline lizards were more abundant at the edges during the dry season, but became more abundant in forest interiors during the wet season. This seasonal variation adds a new dimension to our understanding of edge effects, and carries important practical implications for future studies. The reproductive period of the lizards, which coincides with the rainy season, as well as lower rates of parasitism on anoline lizards near edges, are offered as possible explanations for the observed seasonal pattern.

title: Impacts of timber harvesting on surface activity in terrestrial salamanders

authors.affiliation: Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061-0321

abstract_text: Terrestrial salamanders spend the majority of their time in cool, moist refugia underground, but must surface to forage and breed. Although little is known about their surface activity patterns, abundance is usually inferred by counts of surface active salamanders on wet nights. Recently, such counts have been used to assess the impacts of timber harvesting on terrestrial salamanders. It is assumed in these studies that the percent of the population active on the surface is not altered by the treatment. We tested this assumption by conducting a mark-recapture study on harvested and control plots. We found significantly different proportions active between treatments. At one location, the harvested plot had a lower percent active than its control (Plethodon cinereus: 4.0% vs. 9.2%, p=.021; P. glutinosus: 3.8% vs. 11.7%, p=.091). At the other location, the harvested plots had a higher percent active than their controls (P. cinereus: 4.2% and 3.9% vs. 1.6% and 1.3%, p=.017). At this site, surface counts indicated there were more salamanders on the harvested plots than on the controls, but mark-recapture estimates indicated there were actually twice as many salamanders on the control plots.

title: Gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) movement patterns in large and small habitats: how much land is enough?

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, Auburn University, Auburn AL 36849, USA; JW Jones Ecological Research Center, Ichauway, RR 2 Box 2324, Newton, GA 31770, USA
JW Jones Ecological Research Center, Ichauway, RR 2 Box 2324, Newton, GA 31770, USA

Department of Zoology, Auburn University, Auburn AL 36849, USA

abstract_text: The geographic range of the gopher tortoise has declined due to habitat destruction and fragmentation. Protection strategies typically include preserving patches of habitat or conserving areas occupied by tortoises, even if those areas are restricted in size and quality. However, the patterns observed in these sites can differ from those in large, contiguous areas where conditions may more closely resemble those under which the species evolved. We tracked 131 tortoises via radio-telemetry for one year on an 11,700 ha longleaf pine reserve in southwest Georgia. Male tortoises utilized an average of 9.3 + 4.6 burrows and traveled an average total distance of 83.7 + 73.8 m during the study period. Females utilized 4.8 ± 2.4 burrows and traveled 48.2 ± 57.7 m. The longest movements were 6.4 km by a male tortoise and 480 m by a female. The results of this study emphasize the need to preserve large, contiguous habitats for use by gopher tortoises. Furthermore, it suggests that movement by tortoises is limited in small habitats, especially those surrounded by vast inhospitable areas. Data gathered within large study sites may provide better information for the long-term preservation of this species.

title: Intraspecific phylogeny of the lizard Cnemidophorus sexlineatus: To conserve or not?

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Hofstra University, Hempstead, NY, USA, 11549

abstract_text: Mitochondrial DNA sequence analyses were used to infer phylogeographic relationships among individuals of the lizard species Cnemidophorus sexlineatus, as well as to determine whether a population of C. sexlineatus in Michigan is endemic or recently introduced. Individuals were obtained from Colorado, Oklahoma, Indiana, Michigan, and Florida. A PCR generated fragment which spans the mtDNA ND3 to ND4 gene region, and including the Arginine tRNA, was sequenced for each individual. Sceloporus grammicus and C. gularis sequences were used as outgroups. The preliminary data cannot rule out the possibility that the Michigan population is endemic. The Florida individuals are in a clade basal to a clade that contains Michigan, Indiana, and Oklahoma individuals. Sequence divergence values of the Michigan specimens range from 1.2% to 5.8%. The Indiana and Oklahoma specimens have sequence divergence values of 1.6% to 2.3% and 1.1% to 1.5% respectively. One Colorado sample forms a clade with the C. gularis sample, its sequence divergence is 8.3%.

title: Genetic diversity in drought-impacted populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach CA 90840-3702 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach CA 90840-3702 USA

abstract_text: Populations that experience a large reduction in effective size are expected to exhibit a bottleneck effect which will include loss of heterozygosity and loss of alleles. Populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida, in Central and Southern California were impacted by an extended drought that occurred from 1987-1992 and exhibited local population size decreases up to 85% during this period. I examined changes in genetic diversity in four populations of C. marmorata in the drought affected area by comparing microsatellite DNA allele frequencies from tissue samples collected before and after this drought period. Genotypes of five microsatellite loci were determined to assess the genetic diversity within these samples. Heterozygosity was used as a measurement of genetic diversity. Although no significant decline in heterozygosity was shown in the five loci, there was a decrease in the number of alleles present in the most severely impacted population. Since most individuals that were present in the post-drought samples were survivors of the drought, the first sign of decreased genetic diversity would be the loss of alleles. Changes in the level of genetic diversity (heterozygosity) would only be detectable in subsequent post-drought generations.

title: Amphibian abundance and community structure in fragmented peat bogs

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, B3H 4J1

abstract_text: Peatlands are increasingly exploited in Europe and North America due to the demand for peat in horticulture. As a result, these wetlands are threatened, particularly in New Brunswick and Quebec, North America's principal peat producers. I used drift fences and pitfall traps to investigate amphibian populations in pristine bogs and disturbed bogs (i.e., bog remnants adjacent to peat harvesting operations) of southeastern New Brunswick. Results following 20,592 trap nights indicate that species richness is higher in pristine bogs than disturbed bogs (range 2-7 spp.). Rana clamitans was the only species sensitive to peat harvesting, while the abundance of Rana sylvatica, Rana pipiens, Bufo americanus americanus and Rana septentrionalis did not differ between pristine bogs and bog fragments. Captured individuals consisted almost exclusively of ranid juveniles in both types of bogs. These data show that peat bog harvesting has a definite influence on adjacent amphibian communities. However, additional work will be needed to differentiate natural population fluctuations from the impacts of peat harvesting on amphibian movements and resource (i.e., bog ponds) utilization.

title: Forest canopy closure and dispersal by pool-breeding amphibians

authors.affiliation: Department of Wildlife Ecology, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, 04469, USA
Department of Wildlife Ecology, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, 04469, USA

abstract_text: For amphibians that breed in temporary pools, juvenile dispersal is an important life history movement linking the aquatic habitat of larvae to the surrounding forest habitat occupied by most adults. We examined whether selection occurs for closed-canopy conditions during dispersal using pitfall traps and drift fences to sample naturally occurring, upland populations of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) and spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) along recently created forest-clearcut edges in central Maine. Habitat preferences during dispersal were further investigated using an experimental approach that quantified the movements of newly metamorphosed wood frogs cultured in artificial pools located along an abrupt forest-powerline edge. Among natural populations the abundance of juveniles and adults of both species declined sharply across a gradient running from relatively mature forest-interior habitat (70-90 years old) to recently clearcut habitat (2-11 years old). Similarly, in the powerline experiment, juvenile wood frogs showed a dispersal preference for closed-canopy habitat immediately upon metamorphosis, with the highest capture rates occurring in microhabitats characterized by dense foliage in both the understory and canopy layers. Our results suggest that populations of wood frogs, spotted salamanders, and other vernal pool breeding amphibian species are likely to benefit from efforts to maintain connectivity between upland forest habitats and aquatic breeding sites.

title: Ephemeral aquatic habitats in tallgrass prairie: abiotic changes over time and their effects on developmental rate of western chorus frogs

authors.affiliation: Division of Biology, 232 Ackert Hall, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas 66506 USA

abstract_text: Bison wallows and intermittent streams were sampled weekly in spring 1996 and 1997 on Konza Prairie Research Natural Area, Kansas. We monitored water chemistry and development of western chorus frogs (Pseudacris triseriata) as these aquatic habitats dried. Abiotic factors temporally were more variable in bison wallows than in intermittent streams even after flow stopped. Dissolved oxygen and ammonium fluctuated diurnally in wallows, but remained stable in intermittent streams until just before drying. Water temperature and pH were correlated negatively to water volume in wallows, but not in streams. Eggs in bison wallows hatched at Gosner stages 21 and 22 within 4 to 8 days after laying, whereas eggs in intermittent streams hatched in 14 days at about Gosner stage 21. The majority of tadpoles in wallows reached Gosner stages 38 to 42 in 6 weeks, when wallows dried. In contrast, tadpole development in streams progressed no further than stage 25 until flow ceased in streams, and no tadpoles developed beyond stage 41 when the streams dried after 16 weeks. Differences in developmental rates of these frogs likely result from differences in water temperature and chemistry between ephemeral aquatic habitats found in wallows and streams.

title: The post-breeding migration of the European common frog, Rana temporaria, in relation to landscape structure and seasonal weather

authors.affiliation: Ecology Building, Lund University, 223 62 Lund, Sweden

abstract_text: The post-breeding migration of Rana temporaria was studied by means of radio tracking over three years. One site consisted of an extensive ungrazed, uncut moist meadow where suitable foraging habitats and the breeding site were all contiguous with each other, while in another site suitable habitats were separated by cultivated fields. The study period of the first year coincided with a drought, while the study periods of the following two years had above normal precipitation. This enabled a factorial analysis of the effects of seasonal weather, landscape type and sex on migratory behavior. In the farmland site and during the wet years frogs moved farther from their breeding pond and sources of open water, changed position more often and made longer movements when position was changed. In the farmland site frogs also migrated farther and did so more directly. Nearly all differences between sites were more noticeable during the wet year. There were no significant differences between the sexes, neither were any of the differences between habitats or wet and dry years sex dependent. These migration patterns are discussed in terms of the effects of habitat fragmentation on species survival and the consequences for dispersal between breeding populations.

title: Influence of weather variables on movement patterns of the Northwestern salamander (Ambystoma gracile)

authors.affiliation: University of Washington, Box 352100, Seattle, WA USA

abstract_text: The influence of weather on salamander breeding activity has been well documented. However, weather influence on specific movement patterns is not yet well understood. I investigated the influence of weather variables on movements of Northwestern salamanders. Radio-tracking was conducted during the winter when this species is most active. Both non-breeding and breeding migration movements were observed. Movements were significantly correlated with both temperature increase and rain onset. This relationship was strongest when a cold, dry period was followed by a warm, wet period. Movements began when daily temperatures rose above a mean of 5°C and a minimum of 0°C, and more than 20mm of rain had fallen within the last 24 hours. During these periods most radio-tagged salamanders moved within 48 hours of the weather change and of each other. Breeding migration movements were also correlated with this type of weather change and migration onset invariably began within 48 hours of the first winter thaw. Subsequent cold, dry periods were observed to temporarily suspend migrational movements. During extended periods of warm rainy weather, correlations between weather variables and movements were much weaker and tended to be better explained by individual salamander movement frequency patterns.

title: Nitrate pollution: A serious threat to amphibian survival

authors.affiliation: Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment Canada, Box 5050, Burlington, Ontario, L7R 4A6
Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment Canada, Box 5050, Burlington, Ontario, L7R 4A6
Ecosystem Health Division, Environment Canada, Box 5050, Burlington, Ontario, L7R 4A6

abstract_text: Nitrogen pollution from anthropogenic sources enters water bodies through runoff associated with nitrate fertilization, livestock, precipitation, and effluents from industrial, human and animal wastes. This review assesses the potential for nitrate to affect amphibian populations by comparing environmental concentrations of nitrate in North American waters to nitrate concentrations known to cause toxicity to captive amphibians and other species that play an important role in amphibian ecology. Lethal and sublethal effects in amphibians are detected at nitrate concentrations between 2.5 and 100 mg/L. We found environmental concentrations of nitrate in watersheds throughout North America from <1 to >100 mg/L. Furthermore, amphibian food (insects) and predators (fish) are also affected by these elevated levels of nitrate in surface waters. From this we conclude that nitrate concentrations in watersheds in North America are high enough to cause death and developmental anomalies in amphibians. In the interim, use of vegetated buffer strips adjacent to water courses can reduce nitrogen contamination of surface waters. Ultimately, there is a need to reduce the use of fertilizers, control the run-off of human and livestock waste and establish and enforce water quality guidelines for nitrate for the protection of aquatic life.

title: Relation of catch per unit of effort and floodplain lakes area in Amazon

authors.affiliation: Programa de Pós-Graduação em Ecologia de Ambientes Aquáticos Continentais, Nupélia - Núcleo de Pesquisas em Limnologia, Ictiologia e Aquicultura, UEM - Universidade Estadual de Maringá

abstract_text: The floodplain area of 32 lakes in Lower Solimões River (Amazon) was quantified using a radar image SAR (JERS-1) in order to stablish correlations among these areas and the catch per unit of effort - CPUE (total and by species) in the lakes (effort unit = fisherman numbers x fishery days). Results showed correlation between the lake area and its floodplain area (n=32; Pearson r; p<0.05) while there was a weak correlation of meander number and lakes floodplain area (n=32; r=0.4, ns), and the lake perimeter was correlated with all variables. Catch data shows that just CPUE total was correlated with the floodplain area (Spearman r=0.69; p<0.05; n=8). Lacustrine species and riverine-lacustrine species did not show correlation with the others variables (floodplain area, lake area, perimeter and meander number). However, since Amazon fishes distribution is dependent on many others variables (floodplain forest size and diversity, ecosystem primary production, etc.) those correlations need to be investigated based on larger sample size in order to determinate standards.

title: Artisanal fisheries in a urban reservoir: catch, effort and fishing strategies (Billings reservoir, São Paulo, Brazil)

authors.affiliation: Programa de Pós-Graduação em Ecologia, UNICAMP - Universidade Estadual de Campinas; present address: Nupélia - Núcleo de Pesquisas em Limnologia, Ictiologia e Aquicultura, UEM - Universidade Estadual de Maringá
Depto. de Ecologia, UNESP - Universidade Estadual Paulista

abstract_text: Billings reservoir (127 km2, 23° 42' - 23° 45'S; 46° 27' - 46° 22'W) is the largest water body in the metropolitan region of São Paulo (Brazil). Its building started in 1925 in order to supply the city of São Paulo with electricity. During many years it presented low environmental quality due to the reception of organic sewage from the metropolitan region. Nowadays, it has multiple uses. An intense artisanal fishery activity is present, with 191 fishermen. Landings were recorded daily during a year (1996). During this period 147,593 kg of fish were caught in 3,515 fishing trips by 21.5 fishermen/month in average, with a yield of 42 kg/trip and 572 kg/fisherman/month. The main commercial species caught were Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus (81.4% of landings in weight), an introduced species, 'lambari' Astyanax eigenmanniorum (13.0%) and four other species. Tilapias were caught with castnets and beating gillnets, the other species were caught with gillnets. Through a Principal Component Analysis it was possible to detect two main groups of fishermen considering the fisheries strategies, those who explore only tilapias and those who explore also the other species, related mainly to the ownership of the gears. The low richness and high dominance of few species on landings are indicative of communities under stressing condition. The dominance of Nile tilapia is attributable to a combination of factors as ability to consume plankton and tolerance to low dissolved oxygen contents. abstract_text: Floodplain fishes in the mid-upper Rio Negro are exploited as ornamental fishes to provide subsistence to 3000 people in Barcelos, Amazonas (pop. 12,000; area 122,490 km2). title: Response of salamander distribution to forest canopy gaps created by selective timber harvesting

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Albany University, Albany, NY 12206 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, SUNY at Cortland, Cortland, NY 13045 USA

abstract_text: Selective timber harvesting (removal of individual trees or small groups of trees), which creates gaps in the forest canopy, is widely practiced in public and private forests. However, the effects of this technique on herpetofaunal populations has been incompletely studied. We examined the effect of forest canopy gaps, created by selective harvesting, on the distribution of the northern redback salamander, Plethodon cinereus, in a maple-hemlock forest in central New York State. Distributions of individual salamanders were determined by searching 1 m x 1 m quadrats along transects extending from the center of gaps into the surrounding forest. In the first year following harvest, we found that salamander distributions did not indicate significant movement from or avoidance of gap sites. However, salamander densities were somewhat elevated on the edges of gaps. Data for the second year following harvest are being analyzed.

title: A new database available for herpetological research: Natural history and geographic distribution records from Herpetological Review

abstract_text: We entered citation information for all natural history and geographic distribution records from Herpetological Review (HR), from its first issues to the present. Citations include authors, species, keywords, and locality information. The HR database is available to anyone with WWW access, and can be searched in a variety of ways. For example, when a herpetologist finds a specimen believed to be new for a county, it is now easy to determine if the species has already been reported for that region in HR. title: Recreational freshwater fishing in southwestern Australia

authors.affiliation: Murdoch University, Perth, Western Australia, 6150

abstract_text: The south-west coast of Australia (Darling Botanical District), as defined by the 800mm isohyet, has an area of some 160,000 square kilometres and 19 distinct river drainage basins. In comparison to habitats of southeastern Australia and the Northern Hemisphere, southwestern Australia has a much reduced aquatic faunal diversity: the freshwaters of this region contain only 10 species of native fishes, of which eight are endemic. With the exception of Tandanus bostocki (a freshwater catfish) none of these species typically exceed 140mm in total length. This very low number of freshwater fish species in southwestern Australian waters is thought to be a result of the regions arid past climate, insular nature, low and relatively featureless topography, and low productivity of its aquatic habitats. The regions recreational freshwater fishery currently comprises the introduced perch (Perca fluviatilis) and trouts (Salmo trutta, Oncorhynchus mykiss), and the native decapod, Cherax tenuimanus, the third largest freshwater crayfish. Preliminary data suggests the temperate climate of the south-west promotes fast growth-rates of perch, yet shortens the period during which their spawning is successful, relative to Northern Hemisphere populations. This paper also discusses the likely impact of P. fluviatilis on the established C. tenuimanus fishery, given that at times P. fluviatilis preys almost exclusively on this crayfish species.

title: Combining herpetofaunal education and conservation efforts in the NY State amphibian and reptile Atlas

title: The fish survey: A key management component for the Canadian environmental effects monitoring program

abstract_text: In 1992, the Canadian government passed amendments to the Pulp and Paper Effluent Regulations (PPER) under the Fisheries Act, which included a requirement for mills to conduct an Environmental Effects Monitoring (EEM) program. abstract_text: Avon Park Air Force Range is a federal military reservation occupying 42,900 hectares in Florida's Greater Everglades Region. As part of an aquatic faunal survey (1995-1997), we documented presence of 44 fish species (representing 17 fish families), eight nonindigenous, and one nonindigenous clam and two native crayfishes. Introduced foreign species captured in the area included walking catfish (Clarias batrachus), blue tilapia (Oreochromis aureus), grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) and Asian clam Corbicula fluminea. Two natives, eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki) and least killifish (Heterandria formosa), were by far the most abundant and widespread fishes. Compared with much of Florida, anthropogenic impacts range from low to moderate (e.g., cattle throughout, water diversion in some sections, periodic artillery fire in a few areas). Relative to many environments in peninsular Florida, numbers and densities of nonindigenous fishes in the range are low.

title: Estimates of daily ration and a bioenergetic model for the blacknose shark, Carcharhinus acronotus

Biology Department, University of Mississippi, University, MS 38677, USA

abstract_text: Daily ration estimates and bioenergetic models for blacknose sharks, Carcharhinus acronotus, were developed from laboratory experiments on metabolism and growth at 28±2.0°C. Daily ration was estimated for sharks 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, and 3.5 kg using the equation of Winberg (1956). Daily ration (%body weight/day) decreased with body size and was estimated as 1.56 for smallest sharks and 0.87 for largest sharks based on a diet of menhaden, Brevoortia spp. General energy budgets were constructed for each size class. Routine metabolism generally accounted for the largest percentage of the energy budget but differed among size class and increased with body size from 60% of the energy budget in small sharks (0.5-0.8 kg) to 71% for the largest sharks. title: Modulation of the feeding behavior of the horn shark Heterodontus francisci

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida 33620 USA
Department of Biology, University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida 33620 USA

abstract_text: Many fishes are capable of modulating prey capture behavior according to prey size or elusivity. The physical attributes of the prey appear to affect attack behavior, but factors such as position or location of prey may also be important. This study tests the hypothesis that capture behavior can be modulated according to prey accessibility. Using a high-speed video kinematic analysis, prey capture events are examined for the horn shark, Heterodontus francisci. Each individual encounters three feeding situations: (1) squid pieces resting freely on a platform; (2) attached to a platform; and (3) fitted snugly in a tube. Using suction behavior, H. francisci successfully captures prey in each feeding situation with a common series of kinematic events. However, repeated bites with palatoquadrate protrusion occur during attached feedings, and the labial cartilages extend to form a seal around the tube opening during tube feedings. Average bite duration for three individuals is approximately 124 ms, although significant inter-individual variation is observed. Preliminary analyses show that H. francisci is capable of modulating the duration of some kinematic events during capture, such as mandible elevation and palatoquadrate protrusion/retraction, according to the accessibility of the prey.

title: The effects of scale on the feeding kinematics of the nurse shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum

abstract_text: Successful inertial suction feeding depends, in part, on the speed of the feeding sequence. One factor important to the speed of this behavior is the size of the animal. The effects of scale on the muscular dynamics of aquatic vertebrates are still uncertain. We present data on the scaling of the prey capture kinematics of the nurse shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum, an inertial suction feeder. Morphometrics of the head and feeding apparatus were analyzed in twelve specimens ranging from 71 to 244 cm TL. These data indicated isometric growth of the feeding apparatus. The kinematics of prey capture in another twelve specimens (33 to 268 cm) were recorded with high speed video and subsequently analyzed. The maximal excursions of angular variables remained constant through ontogeny, while the maxima of the linear excursions increased. The time required to reach the maximal excursions of the kinematic variables also increased with increasing animal size. The slopes of the log-transformed data were not significantly different from 0.333, thus these data are consistent with a model of muscular scaling initially proposed for largemouth bass by Richard and Wainwright (1995). This pattern of scaling does not appear to apply to sharks in general.

title: Food habits of the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis), dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus), Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terranovae), and the sand tiger (Carcharias taurus) from the northwest Atlantic Ocean

abstract_text: Diet and feeding habits of the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis), Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terranovae), dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and the sand tiger (Carcharias taurus) were investigated through analysis of stomach contents. Diet in M. canis was relatively homogeneous and was dominated by crustaceans, consisting mostly of rock crabs, Cancer irroratus. Nonetheless, these data suggested that both species are generalized feeders and consume a variety of teleost and elasmobranch prey. title: Kin recognition, sexual selection, and mate choice in toads

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand

abstract_text: Long-term field studies of sexual selection in the explosively breeding American toad, Bufo americanus, reveal only weak evidence of non-random mating based on size. Although advantages may accrue to females that breed with larger males, levels of male-male competition and opportunities for female choice vary. High levels of natal philopatry predict that close inbreeding should be common. Genetic analyses suggest to the contrary that: (1) in natural populations toads largely avoid close inbreeding, and (2) males' advertisement calls encode information about their genetic identities. To examine whether females can assess their relatedness to males by hearing their calls, I conducted laboratory playback experiments. The responses of female subjects to males' calls, broadcast alternately, were analysed as a function of their relatedness to each of the males (determined by multilocus DNA fingerprinting). Females discriminated between calls based on kinship, consistently orienting toward calls of the genetically less similar male. Responses were similar to field-recorded calls and to synthesised calls (controlling for call duration and number of pulses). Females showed no preference if equally related to each calling male. These results suggest that mate choice is more strongly influenced by selection to avoid close inbreeding than by sexual selection for other characters.

title: Historical influences on receiver biases: Artificial neural network models of call recognition in the tungara frog, Physalaemus pustulosus

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712 USA

abstract_text: Studies employing historical methods have shown that preexisting biases in the sensory systems of females are capable of driving the evolution of male traits. I used artificial neural network models - computer simulations emulating real nervous systems - to test whether receiver biases could be directly influenced by the evolutionary history of the female sensory apparatus. Neural networks were given an evolutionary history approximating that of the tungara frog, or one of various control histories. I found that not only does evolutionary history influence receiver biases, but that networks with a history approximating that of the tungara frog were best at predicting female responses to many novel heterospecific calls. The neural networks demonstrate patterns of preference that are clearly vestiges of past selection pressures, and make novel predictions about the preferences of real females.

title: The influence of evolutionary history on signal recognition in tungara frogs

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin TX 78712 USA
Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, 900 Jefferson Drive, Suite 2207, Washington DC 20560

abstract_text: We have been using the advertisement call system of tungara frogs (Physalaemus pustulosus) and their close relatives to attempt to understand the evolution of communication systems. We have analyzed the advertisement calls and phylogenetic relationships of members of the Physalaemus pustulosus species group and three other congeners as outgroups. Using these data we have estimated calls at ancestral nodes and tested tungara frog female preferences for these calls. Here we address the following questions: (1) How conservative is the evolution of various call characters; (2) How do individual call characters influence advertisement call recognition (heterospecific call versus white noise) and discrimination (heterospecific call versus conspecific call); and, (3) Does the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character differentially influence call recognition and discrimination. Our results suggest that: (1) calls do not evolve as tightly coordinated suites of characters, but instead are arrays of more or less plesiomorphic or derived characters; (2) that call discrimination and recognition might be influenced differently by some call characters than others; and, (3) that the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character might have some effect on these tasks.

title: Visual signaling in anuran amphibians

abstract_text: Visual displays are known in both intra- and intersexual anuran communication. We compare the patterns of visual signaling among seven anuran families and discuss the ecological contexts in which they may have evolved. We classified visual cues used during intraspecific interactions as discrete character states and mapped them onto a phylogenetic tree based on morphological characters. Groups of behavioural patterns are apparent and closely but not exclusively associated with anuran families. By adding ecological characteristics and geographic distributions of the involved species to the matrix, the resulting patterns suggest visual displays to be more similar between species of the same family. As striking exceptions, similar displays are performed by two across-family groups of species. Diurnal, neotropical leaf-litter inhabitants and mainly aposematic species in the Brachycephalidae, Bufonidae and Dendrobatidae exhibit an impressive variety of visual displays involving predominantly anterior parts of the body. Stream-side breeding, cryptic species in the Leptodactylidae, Myobatrachidae, Hylidae and Ranidae constitute another probably convergent group, which includes both nocturnal and diurnal species exposed to constant high ambient noise levels. They perform conspicuous visual displays by extending or 'flagging' the posterior limbs. However, Hyla parviceps and Phyllomedusa spp., which advertise and breed at ponds, perform similar displays. The observed patterns suggest that complex visual communication may have evolved under two ecological scenarios. One is associated with the shift to diurnality and the other with breeding at tropical mountain streams. (Foot-flagging displays of Hylodes asper and Staurois latopalmatus are shown in film and video scenes)

title: Corneal pathology associated with the attachment of Ommatokoita elongata (Copepoda: Lernaepodidae) (Grant) to the cornea of Greenland sharks (Somniosus microcephalus)

abstract_text: Eyes from six Greenland sharks, Somniosus microcephalus, infected with the parasitic copepod Ommatokoita elongata were collected in Arctic waters of Victor Bay, Northwest Territories, for study. In addition to opacities associated with copepods at the time of collection, there were several randomly distributed, small, round to irregular, full-thickness corneal opacities which were not associated with copepods. The sclera at the limbus of infected eyes was thickened at the radius corresponding to the feeding range of the copepod. Histologically, corneal epithelial ulceration and heterophilic keratitis, disruption, mineralization, and detachment of Bowman's membrane, thinning, disorganization, mineralization, and fibrosis of the corneal substantia propria, and focal thinning of Descemet's membrane were observed. Mild heterophilic and mononuclear scleritis at the limbus that was continuous with anterior uveitis was also present. We conclude that parasitism by O. elongata could lead to severe visual impairment in Greenland sharks. However, our current research is directed at understanding the physiology of the normal and altered visual apparatus in this species. We are examining retinal enzymes and analyzing the photopigment prosthetic group.

title: The identity of the spotted eagle ray, Aetobatus narinari - a parasitological perspective

authors.affiliation: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA
Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA

abstract_text: Spiral intestines of rays identified as Aetobatus narinari, from the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Thailand and the Timor Sea were examined for tapeworms. Light and electron microscopy of these worms revealed faunal differences among individuals from these localities. Rays from México hosted several different species in the order Tetraphyllidea. Rays from Thailand and Australia hosted species belonging to the order Lecanicephalidea, but, the species of lecanicephalideans differed between the two localities. Although these differences may simply reflect differences in intermediate host availability, it is possible that these data are indicative of differences in the specific identities of the rays. Host morphology seems to support the latter explanation. Although rays from all three localities exhibited dark dorsal surfaces with white spots, size and distribution of these spots differed substantially. Additional differences were seen in the angle of the anterior margin of the pectoral fins and in snout length. Combined these data lead us to suspect that the spotted eagle ray found in the Eastern Pacific might not be conspecific with those found in the two localities in the Indian Ocean. In addition, based on our data, the conspecific identity of the spotted eagle rays from Thailand and Australia is questionable.

title: Identifying cryptic carcharhiniform shark species: tapeworms as diagnostic tools

authors.affiliation: Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA
Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA

abstract_text: Tetraphyllidean tapeworms are restricted to elasmobranch hosts and can be highly host specific; in fact, some species parasitize single species of elasmobranchs and thus may assist in identifying elasmobranch species. Species of the genera Dicranobothrium, Phoreiobothrium, and Platybothrium were found to be restricted in distribution to carcharhiniform sharks and were found in most of the species examined. Our results suggest that the host species examined are parasitized by at least 1 strictly host specific onchobothriid species. In some cases, more than 1 host specific onchobothriid species was found in a single host species. For example, Negaprion acutidens hosted 3 new species of Phoreiobothrium that were not found in the other 30 species of carcharhiniform sharks examined. These results suggest that each carcharhiniform species may possess a unique parasite fauna that could be used as a diagnostic tool for species identification.

title: Buoyancy in deep-sea sharks from the Chatham Rise, New Zealand

authors.affiliation: Zoology Department, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, HI, USA

abstract_text: Although deep-sea sharks approach neutral buoyancy through a large oily liver that contains low-density lipids such as squalene, there have been few comparisons of buoyancy within and among species of sharks. Buoyancy and chemical composition of the liver oil of sharks collected in deep-water trawls from the Chatham Rise, New Zealand were compared. Although there appears to be strong selection for neutral buoyancy in these sharks, buoyancy characteristics of sharks varied with species, size, sex and reproductive state. Livers of smaller sharks contain more squalene and are less dense than livers of larger sharks. However, livers of larger sharks contain a greater proportion of oil than livers of smaller sharks, and the whole body of sharks is nearly uniformly neutrally buoyant regardless of size of shark. Livers of mature male sharks contain more squalene and are less dense than those of mature females, but the non-liver tissue in females is less dense than that of males, and the whole bodies of both sexes are equally neutrally buoyant. Regulation of buoyancy of species of sharks found in shallow water differs considerably from that of deeper species, and appears to rely more on hydrodynamic lift provided by lifting surfaces such as fins.

title: Kinematics of shark pectoral fin movements and their implications for lift-production

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of South Florida, LIF 136, 4202 E. Fowler Ave, Tampa FL 33620 USA

abstract_text: Elasmobranchs, negatively buoyant animals, must produce dynamic lift to avoid sinking. Current models of shark locomotion assume that lift is produced posteriorly by the heterocercal caudal fin and anteriorly by the pectoral fins and head. These two components of lift produce torques at the center of mass that negate one another. All models have assumed that the pectoral fins are static during swimming. Using a dual video camera system I recorded spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias, swimming in a large flume. Marks placed on the fins divided them into separate segments. Three-dimensional kinematic analyses of these individual segments of the fins and head of the shark demonstrated manipulation of the pectoral fins by the sharks during swimming. The angle of the pectoral fin was modified during steady swimming and was correlated with the position of the caudal fin during its beat. An index of lift was calculated for each fraction of the pectoral fin and head. The head appears to produce significantly more lift during steady swimming and while the animal is ascending in the water column. The negative lift produced by the pectoral fins appears to be important in angling the animal down when it begins a descent.

title: Preliminary analysis of factors influencing swimming speed of the subadult lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris) at Bimini Lagoon, Bahamas

authors.affiliation: Bimini Biological Field Station, Bimini, Bahamas

abstract_text: Influence of time of day, location of shark and tracker experience on swimming speed was examined in seven subadult lemon sharks using speed sensing transmitters. The bioenergetic significance of these trackings will be discussed. Supported by the US Office of Naval Research, the Bimini Biological Field Station and the Earthwatch organization.

title: Odontological variations in the dentition of the manta ray (Manta birostris)

authors.affiliation: 33 Nordica Drive, Croton-on-Hudson, NY 10520 USA

abstract_text: The study of Neogene batoids requires an understanding of extant species. title: Tooth replacement rate of the great white shark, Carcharodon carcharias (Linnaeus, 1758)

abstract_text: Analysis of 31 jaws of Carcharodon carcharias, from specimens ranging in total length from 143.5 to 460.9 cm, finds a range in tooth replacement rate of the Second Lateral tooth family of (Upper Jaw/Lower Jaw) 106.24/113.59 days for young individuals to 225.90/242.18 days for old individuals using the Strasburg Plot Method. title: Trabecular prismatic cartilage: a novel solution to strengthening the jaws of a cartilaginous fish

authors.affiliation: Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, UMASS Amherst, Amherst, MA 01003 USA

abstract_text: A synapomorphy of the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) is that some, or all, of the skeleton is composed of calcified cartilage known as prismatic cartilage. The surface of prismatic cartilage is a mosaic of plates of calcium apatite crystals called tesserae. These tesserae surround a core of hyaline cartilage much as the rind surrounds the pulpy fruit of an orange and serve to stiffen the skeletal element. In both jaw cartilages of the cownose ray, Rhinoptera bonasus, struts of calcification run through the hyaline cartilage core. Cownose rays feed on mollusks, ophiuroids and other hard prey. Tooth plates of adults show distinct wear patterns where the prey is usually crushed. A sagittal section through this 'trabecular cartilage' shows that the struts are positioned so as to prevent buckling in this area. The common ancestor of cartilaginous and bony fishes is thought to have had a bony endoskeleton. The lamellar bone of the tesserae and vertebrae of chondrichthians is evidence that the skeleton has not lost osteogenic potential entirely. The data presented here indicate that a novel developmental and biochemical process is also at work in the cartilage. Data from neonate individuals indicates that the process of trabeculation is not epigenetic, but rather is part of a fixed developmental pattern. Bone is typically strengthened through endosteal deposition and trabeculation. In a remarkable example of convergence, multiple layers of tesserae and strut formation serve the same purpose in cartilage.

title: Consequences of pesticide accumulation in anuran populations

title: Effects of clearcutting on amphibian and reptile communities of temporary ponds in a managed pine flatwoods

authors.affiliation: USDI, US Geological Survey, BRD, 320 Laurel Valley Road, Townsend, TN 37882

abstract_text: The herpetofaunal community of a slash pine flatwoods ecosystem of north-central Florida was monitored from August 1993 through August 1994, October 1995 through September 1996, and November 1996 onward. Drift fences with funnel traps and PVC pipe refugia were used to gather baseline data on the herpetofaunal community using nine temporary ponds and the adjacent uplands, before and after a timber harvest. Study ponds ranged in size from 0.01 - 0.71 ha. Forty-five species (16 amphibian, 29 reptile) were recorded. Effects of clearcutting and site preparation included significant short-term changes in both amphibian and reptile abundance. As compared with the control, amphibian numbers were higher on the clearcut in the first two summers post-harvest (P < 0.001, P = 0.0137, respectively). Reptile numbers were higher on the clearcut in the first summer (P < 0.001). In year three (1997) for amphibians and year two (1996) for reptiles, relative abundance on the clearcut site returned to numbers comparable to those observed on the control. Movement of amphibians and reptiles was documented with distances ranging from 16 - 692 m (Mean = 98.1, n = 47, SD = 145.9). Thus some amphibians and reptiles are using large areas of the flatwoods, including upland habitat and one or more ponds.

title: Effects of selection logging on the relative abundance of breeding amphibians within tolerant hardwood forests of Ontario

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: Many of Ontario's amphibian species occur in forested areas of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence region. These species are potentially susceptible to habitat disturbance and alteration associated with selection logging protocols used to harvest uneven-aged, tolerant hardwood forests in these areas. In 1995, I began a research program to determine whether, and if so, by what mechanism(s), selection logging affects amphibian diversity and abundance at breeding sites. In 1996 and 1997, I compared amphibian abundance concurrently with habitat characteristics of: (a) 10 ephemeral breeding pools adjacent to logging roads, (b) 10 ephemeral breeding pools within forest stands logged 2-3 years prior to being surveyed, and (c) 10 ephemeral breeding pools in forest stands that had been left undisturbed for at least 30-40 years. Results of nocturnal, time constrained surveys of breeding adult abundance at these pools suggest that selection logging does not affect the abundance of breeding adults as a group. However, when I analyzed data for each species separately, I found that although selection logging does not appear to affect the relative abundance of Spring Peepers, Wood Frogs appear to be more abundant in undisturbed forests than in logged forests during the early part of the breeding season. The relative abundance of American Toads was consistently higher in breeding pools within logged forests. Stepwise multiple regression analysis suggests that variation in amphibian abundance can be explained best by variation in the duration of these ephemeral pools.

title: How important is statistical power when testing hypotheses of amphibian decline?

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1
Canadian Wildlife Service, Box 5050, Burlington, Ontario L7R 4N0
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: The jargon of statistical power has invaded the vocabulary of almost every conservation biologist despite being largely absent from the literature as applied methodology. With respect to amphibian population monitoring, power refers to the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis (that there is no decline) when the alternative hypothesis is true (a decline is occurring). Clearly we want high power in our monitoring programs so as to minimize the chance of making a Type II error (i.e., failing to detect a decline that is occurring). However, many amphibian monitoring programs likely do not have the necessary power to satisfactorily reduce the possibility that actual declines are occurring, even though some studies suggest stability and have data-sets that exceed 10 years. Here, we review the concepts of statistical power as they apply to detecting population declines. We then calculate an estimate of power for long-term data on bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) to investigate the problems associated with maximizing power in amphibian monitoring programs. We also comment on how an understanding of power should influence both the design of monitoring programs and management expectations.

title: Translocation of amphibians into mitigated and existing wetlands - a review of a new protocol

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Frostburg State University, Frostburg, MD 21532 USA
Department of Biology, Frostburg State University, Frostburg, MD 21532 USA

abstract_text: Previous amphibian relocation, repatriation, and translocation programs have proven most successful when introducing individuals in early developmental stages. Over the next 2 years, we will introduce egg masses of target amphibian species into artificial ponds in mitigated and existing wetland areas at Rocky Gap State Park. Three pairs of constructed ponds (approximately 18.5 m2) are arranged so one shallow pond (< .4m in depth) and one deep pond (> .45m in depth) comprise each pair. The shallow ponds will facilitate establishment of small, less abundant anuran species by excluding larger species with longer developmental stages. To monitor migration all ponds are encircled by drift fencing with both pitfall and funnel traps. Introduced egg masses will be monitored by recording percent hatching success and larvae will be monitored by tracking tadpole survivorship via weekly population estimates using a quadrat box sampling technique. Metamorphosed individuals captured while dispersing from the ponds will be marked with toe-clipping to determine if they return to breed in subsequent seasons. Additional marking schemes include freeze branding metamorphosed salamanders and photoidentification of anurans. Additional constructed ponds in adjacent areas are being monitored for unaided colonization.

title: Amphibians and reptiles of the Georgian Bay islands

authors.affiliation: Office of the Secretary of State, Edifice Jules Leger, 11th Floor, Hull, Quebec, K1A 0M5
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: Forming a large eastern embayment on Lake Huron, Georgian Bay comprises a body of water approximately the same size as the state of Vermont. Bounded in the west by the limestone arc of the Niagara escarpment, and in the east by the Canadian Shield, the Bay encompasses some of Ontario's most spectacular scenery. It is also one of the province's richest areas for amphibians and reptiles, with 35 species recorded. In Georgian Bay Islands National Park, Beausoleil Island alone, at an area of 1100 ha, supports 32 species. Among the resident herpetofauna are the regionally rare Spotted Turtle, Eastern Hognose Snake, Eastern Fox Snake and Eastern Massasauga. During the summers of 1995 and 1996, herpetofaunal surveys were conducted on 43 of the approximately 30,000 islands in Georgian Bay. This talk will provide an overview of the varied habitats and herpetofauna of this region, as well as a discussion of the biogeographic points of interest.

title: Comparisons of assimilation efficiency and gut characteristics in two species of herbivorous damselfishes (Stegastes dorsopunicans and S. planifrons)

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Box 5640, NAU, Flagstaff AZ, 86011-5640 USA

abstract_text: As consumers of 60-99% of reef primary productivity, herbivorous fishes occupy a pivotal role in channeling energy along the reef food chain. I examined feeding physiology and ecology of two territorial herbivorous damselfishes commonly found among the coral reefs of the San Blas Archipelago, Republic of Panama. I measured gut length, gut retention time, and total and nutrient-specific assimilation efficiencies and made interspecific comparisons between the dusky damselfish (S. dorsopunicans) and the threespot damselfish (S. planifrons). Relative gut length is significantly different between the two damselfish species. Dusky damselfish have a relative gut length ratio (gut length/standard length) of 1.20 and a Zihler index ((gut length/(weight^1/3)) of 3.42. Values for the threespot damselfish are 3.01 and 8.24 respectively. Despite striking differences in RGL and ZI, the gut retention time is the same for both species. Additionally, only protein assimilation efficiency (and thus total assimilation efficiency) varies between species; significantly more protein is assimilated by the threespot damselfish than the dusky damselfish. These results have several important implications. First, as both species feed on the same algal diet, the greater assimilation efficiency of the threespot damselfish may translate into faster growth rates and greater reproductive capacity. Second, it has long been held that relative gut length ratios of herbivorous fishes fall between 2 and 21, with most herbivorous damselfishes in the range of 5. The significantly lower relative gut length of dusky damselfish, unquestionably an herbivore, challenges trophic classifications based on relative gut length ratios. Third, gut morphologies are often used in phylogenetic analyses. These two damselfish are closely related congeners yet their gut morphologies vary significantly. This questions the applicability of such characters in phylogenetic analyses.

title: Intraspecific molecular systematics of the sabine shiner, Notropis sabinae (Teleostei: Cyprinidae)

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Saint Louis University, 3507 Laclede Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63103-2010 USA

abstract_text: Prior to 1991, the sabine shiner, Notropis sabinae, was known only from drainages west of the Mississippi River. In the process of describing the Yazoo shiner, N. rafinesquei, Suttkus noted the presence of N. sabinae within the Yazoo River, a system which lies east of the Mississippi River. Further sampling uncovered yet another eastern population within the Big Black River system. Upon preliminary examination, the latter population appears to show morphological novelties for this group. Given the diversity exhibited among populations of N. sabinae, a genetic data set was assembled to aid in defining operational taxonomic units (OTUs, sensu Mayden and Wood, 1995) within this species, and to suggest avenues for further study. Sequences were collected from the mitochondrial cytochrome b gene from individuals representing the geographic range of this species and were subjected to phylogenetic and population-level analyses. In all analyses, the Big Black River population was strongly supported as monophyletic and distinct from any other population.

title: Quick and accurate identification of triggerfishes (Balistidae) using PCR with species-diagnostic mitochondrial (12S/16S) primers

authors.affiliation: Nova Southeastern University, Oceanographic Center, 8000 Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA

abstract_text: Identification of ichthyoplankton (eggs, larvae, and juveniles) can be a challenging task due to their small sizes and dynamic development. This problem is particularly acute for tropical and subtropical ichthyoplankton, most of which can be identified to family-level only. As part of a broader initiative to develop molecular markers for tropical and subtropical fish identification, we report on the utility of mitochondrial ribosomal gene sequences for triggerfish species identification. A 1,510 bp fragment, containing portions of the mitochondrial ribosomal genes (12S, 16S) and the complete tRNA valine gene, was sequenced from six triggerfish species (4 genera) inhabiting the western central Atlantic Ocean. Forty-three sequences were examined to assess intra- and interspecific variation. Intraspecific differences were minor (less than 0.5%); however, sufficient interspecific differences occur within this locus to allow the design of robust species-specific PCR primers. When tested in a multiplex PCR assay, these primers yielded species-diagnostic size fragments that unambiguously identified all 4 genera and 4 of the 6 species. Distinction between the two Canthidermis congeners (0.9% interspecific variation) was not possible using this approach; however, these congeners were readily distinguished using RFLP analysis of the PCR amplicon. We suggest that molecular genetic approaches can provide a robust and rapid method to tackle long-standing problems in the identification of fish species.

title: Evolution of karyotypes, reproductive organs, and trophic structures in the Goodeidae (Pisces: Cyprinodontiformes) based on nuclear and mitochondrial DNA phylogenies: The continuing saga

authors.affiliation: The University of Alabama, Department of Biological Sciences, Box 870345, Tuscaloosa, Alabama 35487-0345 USA

abstract_text: The family Goodeidae is a distinct North American lineage of freshwater fishes and is comprised of two monophyletic subfamilies (Empetrichthyinae and Goodeinae). Empetrichthyinae contains all egg-laying species and Goodeinae contains all viviparous species. The Goodeinae is recognized as a monophyletic group based on the presence of unique morphological traits associated with internal fertilization and viviparity. The classification of goodeids has been based largely on variation of reproductive and trophic characters. A molecular phylogenetic hypothesis is presented based on the cladistic analysis of mtDNA (portions of the 16s rRNA, control region, and cytochrome b genes) and nDNA (a portion of the tyrosine kinase X-src gene) of representative goodeid fishes. The comparative method based on the molecular phylogeny was used to reconstruct the evolution of key characters traditionally used in the classification of the group such as: trophotaeniae (external projections of the embryonic gut that absorb maternal nutrients), karyotypes, and tooth and jaw structures. The phylogeny agrees with some but not all conclusions from earlier studies regarding phylogenetic relationships and reproductive and trophic character evolution.

title: Are you considering transplantation as a management tool? Be cautious - mixing gene pools may be more harmful than helpful due to outbreeding depression

authors.affiliation: The University of Georgia, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802 USA

abstract_text: Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts inbreeding depression (ID) for offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (i.e., OD occurs). Populations of eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms. OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage sections (7 of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.

title: Evolution of the biomechanical attributes of long bones in fish, amphibians, and reptiles

authors.affiliation: Biomechanical Engineering Division, Mechanical Engineering Department, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305-3030 USA

abstract_text: Long bones are the major skeletal elements of vertebrate appendages. The radiations of many vertebrate clades were facilitated by locomotory innovations involving these elements (e.g. the terrestrial diversification of tetrapods) and thus it is necessary to understand how these elements changed biomechanically to more fully understand vertebrate evolution. Biomechanical attributes of long bones such as strength, modulus, and loading conditions are well documented in avian and mammalian taxa. However, data for taxa from outgroup clades are virtually non-existent and the results from the few studies that have been conducted are not in accord with those obtained for bird and mammal bones. In order to provide a better understanding of skeletal evolution, I conducted a series of biomechanical tests on long bones from a diversity of fish, amphibians, and reptiles that possessed basal locomotory attributes within their respective clades. Evolutionary trends were assessed using phylogenetic character analysis. The results suggest: 1) material properties (strength, modulus, and failure strain) did not vary throughout evolution, 2) in vivo strain regimes increased independently in birds and mammals, 3) the capacity of long bones to functionally adapt is a plesiomorphic osteichthyan trait, and 4) size and shape changes were the primary means by which long bones changed to meet evolutionary locomotory challenges.

title: Comparative locomotor kinematics of three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, and D. sabina)

authors.affiliation: University of Chicago, Dept. OBA, 1027 E. 57th, Chicago, IL 60637, USA

abstract_text: Locomotion in stingrays occurs as waves are propagated along their broadly expanded pectoral fins and can range from being undulatory to oscillatory. This study compares swimming behavior in three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, D. sabina) differing in fin design (disc shape) as measured by aspect ratio (AR). Three-dimensional video recordings captured swimming kinematics over a range of velocities for the three species. Results indicate that D. americana (highest AR) has a significantly lower wing beat frequency and lower number of waves than the other two species. Wing amplitude, as a percentage of wing span, differs significantly in T. lymma (highest) and D. sabina (lowest). The results of frequency and number of waves corroborate previous studies suggesting that higher aspect ratio fins tend to have a lower frequency and lower number of waves than low aspect ratio fins; however, the amplitude data does not fit the prediction of high AR fins having greater amplitude. Overall, D. americana falls more toward the oscillatory end of the continuum and T. lymma falls toward the undulatory end, with D. sabina somewhere in between these two.

title: Light attenuating molecules in the lens of the fish eye

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biological Sciences, Univ. of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, 90089; Section of Vertebrates, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, 900 Exposition Blvd., Los Angeles, CA, 90007 USA

abstract_text: The ocular lens of fishes contains mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), which attenuate short wavelengths of light. The causes for the varied distribution of MAAs in the lenses of different fish species are still in question. In this study I examined the lenticular MAA content of 42 flatfish species (order Pleuronectiformes) from nine families to investigate the controlling factors on lens pigmentation and changes in pigmentation during ontogeny. MAAs were actively transported and concentrated by the lens from the surrounding humors in the eye. These MAAs produced two absorbance peaks when analyzed spectrophotometrically, one near 320 nm and another near 360 nm. The relative amounts of different MAAs in the lens was correlated with phylogeny, while the total MAA concentration reflected the depth distribution of each species. Species living in deeper water contained lower concentrations of MAAs. Both the total amount of MAAs and their relative proportions changed during ontogeny. MAAs began accumulating after settlement, and increased in concentration with standard length. The phylogenetic trend in the relative proportion of MAA peaks suggests that lens pigmentation is under genetic control. This control is not exerted by the lens itself, but may occur at the level of food metabolism.

title: The effects of chronic and periodic acute hypoxia on the growth and physiology of juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, Box 7617, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695

abstract_text: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is proving to be one of the most important determinants of juvenile fish growth and survival in our estuaries. Laboratory experiments were conducted to determine the effects of chronic hypoxia and periodic acute hypoxia on the growth, metabolic rate and blood hematocrit of juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma. Fish were maintained in aquaria having constant salinity (15 psu) and temperature (25 °C) and exposed to constant normoxia (6 mg O2 l-1), constant hypoxia (2.75), an intermediate level (4.5), and a diel oscillating treatment (daily mean = 4.5 mg O2 l-1). Results from the blood hematocrit analysis indicate a secondary stress response to the nocturnal hypoxia in the oscillating treatment resulting in increased blood hematocrit levels. Flounder also exhibited limited growth in the low DO treatment (1.9 % Wt d-1, p<0.001) suggesting a species-level limiting oxygen concentration for growth between the low (2.75) and intermediate (4.5) DO levels. Furthermore, fish in the oscillating treatment realized growth similar to the intermediate treatment indicating that daily growth is a function of the daily mean DO concentrations. This hypothesis is supported by the dramatic overcompensation in the afternoon routine respiration rates exhibited by the oscillating treatment. Further work is necessary to address the synergistic effects of temperature and variable DO on the growth and physiology of juvenile estuarine dependent fish.
